candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Convert mixed numbers (and whole numbers when needed) into equivalent improper fractions or equivalent fractional forms suitable for computation, optionally with a specified denominator.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts describe rewriting mixed numbers a b/c as (a·c+b)/c and (when needed) rewriting whole numbers as equivalent fractions; B additionally mentions nonstandard mixed numbers but the core conversion concept is the same.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Determine and use a common denominator (often via LCM) to rewrite fractions as equivalent fractions with the same denominator by scaling numerators and denominators.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts include selecting/computing a common denominator (often LCM) and converting each fraction to an equivalent fraction over that denominator; exclusions consistently separate this from the subtraction step.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Compute the difference of two rational numbers once they are expressed in compatible forms (e.g., same denominator or separated whole and fractional parts).
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts define the actual subtraction operation after compatibility is achieved (subtract numerators over a common denominator or subtract whole and fractional parts separately); B explicitly mentions zero results but that is within the same subtraction concept.

candidate_skills.canonical_definition: Reduce a fraction to lowest terms and/or express an improper fraction as an equivalent mixed number or integer (including identifying whole-number results) when appropriate.
candidate_skills.alignment_notes: All three experts include post-subtraction simplification (reduce to lowest terms) and formatting (improper to mixed number or integer/whole-number identification), clearly separated from finding common denominators or performing subtraction.

alignment_summary: Across codebooks A, B, and C, the same four-step skill progression is present with consistent boundaries: (1) convert mixed/whole numbers to improper/equivalent fractions, (2) find and apply a common denominator via equivalent fractions, (3) perform the subtraction once forms are compatible, and (4) simplify and format the final result. All concepts show full 3/3 consensus with only minor elaborations in B (e.g., nonstandard mixed numbers, explicit zero-result mention) that do not create distinct skill concepts.
